name: Lhasa
info: Lhasa is a city on the Kyi River in the Tibetan Plateau, made the capital of the Tibetan Empire by Songtsen Gampo in the 7th century and the religious and administrative capital of Tibet since the mid-17th century.

facts.founded: Songtsen Gampo moved the capital of the Tibetan Empire to Rasa (Lhasa) and in 637 raised the first structures on the site of the present Potala Palace; he built the Jokhang and Ramoche temples in 641.
facts.where: On the middle reaches of the Lhasa (Kyi) River, a tributary of the Yarlung Zangbo (Brahmaputra), at about 3,650 metres on the Tibetan Plateau, in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China.
facts.known: The Jokhang and Ramoche temples; the Potala Palace; the seat of the Dalai Lamas; the Gelugpa monasteries of Ganden, Sera and Drepung; the Barkhor market and the pilgrim paths around it; Norbulingka; the British expedition of 1904
facts.today: Lhasa is the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region, and the name is also used for the inner urban district of Lhasa City, Chengguan District.

t: Songtsen Gampo made Rasa, later called Lhasa, the capital of the Tibetan Empire in the 7th century and built the Jokhang and Ramoche temples there in 641 to house two Buddha statues.

After the empire fell in the 9th century political power lay elsewhere, but Lhasa became the centre of the Gelugpa school in the 15th century and the capital of the 5th Dalai Lama's government from 1642.
The Qing entered the city in 1720, a British expedition occupied it in 1904, and after 1950 and the flight of the 14th Dalai Lama in 1959 it became the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region in 1965.
dyk: Ancient Tibetan documents call the place Rasa, meaning "goat's place", a herding site. It was renamed Lhasa, "place of gods", when it became the capital and the Jokhang was completed to house a holy statue of the Buddha.

sections.origins:
Lhasa lies in the middle reaches of the Lhasa River, also called the Kyi River or Kyi Chu, a tributary of the Yarlung Zangbo, in the centre of the Tibetan Plateau at about 3,600 metres, with mountains rising to 5,500 metres around it. Ancient Tibetan documents and inscriptions call the place Rasa, "goat's place", a herding site. The name changed to Lhasa, "place of gods", when it was established as the capital of Tibet and the Jokhang was completed to house a holy statue of the Buddha. The name Lhasa is first recorded, as the name of the area's temple of Jowo, in a treaty between China and Tibet of 822 CE.

By the mid-7th century Songtsen Gampo had founded the Tibetan Empire, rising to power in the valley of the Yarlung Tsangpo. After conquering the kingdom of Zhangzhung in the west he moved the capital from Chingwa Taktsé Castle in Chongye County to Rasa, where in 637 he raised the first structures on the site of the present Potala Palace on Mount Marpori. He is said to have married Princess Bhrikuti of Nepal in 639 and Princess Wencheng of the Tang court in 641, and Bhrikuti is said to have converted him to Buddhism. In 641 he built the Jokhang and the Ramoche temple to house two Buddha statues, the Akshobhya Vajra and the Jowo Sakyamuni, which the princesses are said to have brought to his court. In a Tibetan tradition Padmasambhava magically pinned down an earth demoness and built the foundation of the Jokhang over her heart.
sections.growth:
After the empire fragmented, the importance of Lhasa as a religious site grew over the centuries. By the 15th century the city had risen to prominence after Je Tsongkhapa and his disciples founded three large Gelugpa monasteries, Ganden, Sera and Drepung, as part of a puritanical Buddhist revival. The scholarly achievements and political skill of the Gelugpa lineage eventually brought Lhasa back to centre stage.

The 5th Dalai Lama, Lobsang Gyatso (1617 to 1682), moved the centre of his administration to Lhasa in 1642 and Lhasa then became both the religious and the political capital. Reconstruction of the Potala Palace began in 1645 on Red Hill. The Potrang Karpo, the White Palace, was completed in 1648, and the Dalai Lama used the Potala as a winter palace from then on. The Potrang Marpo, the Red Palace, was added between 1690 and 1694, and the Jokhang was greatly expanded around the same time. Some wooden carvings and lintels of the Jokhang date to the 7th century, but the oldest of the city's extant buildings date to this second flowering. Norbulingka, the summer residence of the Dalai Lamas, was built from 1755.

By the end of the 17th century the Barkhor formed a busy market for foreign goods. The Jesuit missionary Ippolito Desideri reported in 1716 that the city had a cosmopolitan community of Mongol, Chinese, Muscovite, Armenian, Kashmiri, Nepalese and northern Indian traders. Tibet exported musk, gold, medicinal plants, furs and yak tails, in exchange for sugar, tea, saffron, Persian turquoise, European amber and Mediterranean coral.
sections.rulers:
Lhasa was the capital of the Tibetan Empire after Songtsen Gampo moved it there. From the fall of the monarchy in the 9th century to the accession of the 5th Dalai Lama the centre of political power in the Tibetan region was not in Lhasa. In 1642 the 5th Dalai Lama unified Tibet and moved his administration there with the help of Güshi Khan of the Khoshut, who remained a largely uninvolved overlord. Historians call the civil administration he and his intimates set up the Lhasa state, and its core leadership the Ganden Phodrang.

The armies of the Qing dynasty entered Lhasa in 1720, and the Qing government sent resident commissioners, the Ambans, to the city. After the Qianlong Emperor suppressed a riot in 1750 he reorganised the Tibetan government and set up the governing council, the Kashag, in Lhasa in 1751. In January 1904 a British expedition captured and briefly occupied the city. Its leader, Sir Francis Younghusband, negotiated the Convention of Lhasa with remaining Tibetan officials after the 13th Dalai Lama had fled to the countryside. The treaty was later repudiated. All remaining Chinese troops left Lhasa after the Xinhai Lhasa turmoil of 1912.

On 2 November 1949 the Tibetan government wrote to Mao Zedong asking for talks; no consensus was reached. On 7 October 1950 the People's Liberation Army launched the Battle of Chamdo, and in April 1951 a Tibetan delegation headed by Ngapo-Ngawang Jigme reached a consensus in Beijing on peace talks. In September 1965 the Tibet Autonomous Region was established with Lhasa as its capital.
sections.life:
Lhasa was a centre of Tibetan Buddhism. In the first half of the 20th century nearly half its population were monks, though that figure may include monks from the surrounding monasteries who came for festivals. Pilgrims walked two sacred circuits: the Barkhor, about one kilometre long around the Jokhang, and the Lingkhor, 8 kilometres long around old Lhasa, the Potala and Chokpori hill. The Barkhor had four large incense burners in the four directions, burning constantly to please the gods protecting the Jokhang. Chokpori held a famous medical school. Twenty-two parks, the lingkas, once surrounded the city, where people picnicked and watched open-air operas on festival days.

The city was not wholly Buddhist. Islam has been present since the 11th century, and two Tibetan Muslim communities lived in Lhasa with their own homes, food, clothing, language, education and trade. Four mosques stand in and around it, the earliest, Khache Lingka, dating to 1650. Most of the Chinese population before 1950 were merchants and officials, and the people of the Lubu section were descendants of Chinese vegetable farmers who came in the 1840s to 1860s after a Chinese official was appointed Amban. Traders from Nepal and Ladakh also lived there.

Figures for the old city's size vary. A census of 1854 gave 42,000, a figure said to have fallen greatly afterwards. The 1910 to 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica put the population at about 30,000 including the lamas, and Hugh Richardson gave 25,000 to 30,000 for 1952, or 45,000 to 50,000 with the great monasteries on its outskirts.
sections.crises:
A Tibetan tradition holds that after Songtsen Gampo's death in 649 Chinese troops invaded and captured Lhasa and burnt the Red Palace. Chinese and Tibetan scholars have noted that the event appears in neither the Chinese annals nor the Tibetan manuscripts of Dunhuang, and one scholar suggested it may derive from an interpolation. In the 9th century Lhasa suffered extensive damage under Langdarma, when sacred sites were destroyed and desecrated and the empire fragmented.

On 11 November 1750 the murder of the regent by the Ambans set off a riot in the city that left more than a hundred people dead, among them the Ambans. In 1904 the British expedition captured the city, and the Xinhai Lhasa turmoil of 1912 ended with the departure of the remaining Chinese troops.

In 1959, following a failed uprising, the 14th Dalai Lama and his associates fled Tibet. Many important sites were damaged or destroyed, mostly but not solely during the Cultural Revolution of the 1960s. The Ramoche temple was gutted and partly destroyed in that decade and its famous bronze statue disappeared; in 1983 its lower part was said to have been found in a Lhasa rubbish tip and its upper half in Beijing. Of the 22 lingkas only three survive, as dormitory blocks, offices and army barracks were built over the rest. Most of the old streets and buildings of the Barkhor have been demolished and replaced, and some buildings there were damaged in the unrest of 2008. A crackdown on protests followed in 2008.
sections.legacy:
Lhasa remains the chief city of Tibetan Buddhism. The Jokhang is for most Tibetans the most sacred and important temple in Tibet and a key centre of pilgrimage for centuries; it is presently controlled by the Gelug school. The Potala Palace was the chief residence of the Dalai Lama. After the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India during the uprising of 1959 the government converted it into a museum, and it was restored between 1989 and 1994. The Potala, the Jokhang and Norbulingka are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Potala was inscribed in 1994. UNESCO has expressed concern about the deterioration of Lhasa's traditional cityscape.

The Lhasa Zhol Pillar below the Potala dates to about 764 CE and carries what may be the oldest known example of Tibetan writing, with the account of a Tibetan general's campaigns against China, including the brief capture of Chang'an in 763. A Monument to the Peaceful Liberation of Tibet was unveiled in Potala Square in May 2002 to mark the 51st anniversary of the Seventeen Point Agreement, with an inscription describing the development of Tibet over fifty years.

Lhasa is the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region. The 2010 census counted 429,104 Tibetans, 76.70 percent of the population, and 121,065 Han Chinese, 21.64 percent. A 2011 book estimated that up to two thirds of the city's residents are non-Tibetan, while the government states that Chengguan District is 63 percent ethnic Tibetan.

summary: Lhasa, on the Kyi River of the Tibetan Plateau, became the capital of the Tibetan Empire under Songtsen Gampo in the 7th century. The 5th Dalai Lama made it the capital of his government in 1642, and since 1965 it has been the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region.
notes: Only the city's own article was available (no lhasa-history file). It is the article on Chengguan District and is thin on 1950 onward; no positions of governments are given beyond the wording of the 2002 monument ('Peaceful Liberation') and the 'Central Government' invitation; I stated the 1950 to 1965 events as dated facts and left out the article's phrases of one side ('At the invitation of the Central Government', 'expressed its hope for a settlement').

START 637: the article says Songtsen Gampo 'raised the first structures' on the Potala site in 637 after moving the capital; the Potala section says he built the first palace in 637. Marriages (639, 641) and Bhrikuti's conversion of him are 'said to' in the article and hedged here. The Padmasambhava demoness story is attributed to tradition.

649 Chinese invasion: given as a Tibetan tradition that scholars doubt, as the article does. The article also says later Tibetan accounts acknowledge the brutality of Chinese forces; I left that sentence out as it is unattributed and tied to the doubted event.
Mentsikhang: the article says founded 1413 and also conceived by the 5th Dalai Lama and completed shortly before 1697; I said only that Chokpori was the site of a famous medical school.

Population: the article gives conflicting figures, including 'about 10,000' (one writer, 1959) against Richardson's 1952 figure; I left the 1959 figure out. The present population figure (2024) and the 2000 figures are left out; the 2010 percentages are given with the 2011 book and the government's 63 percent.
The 1750 riot: the article says the regent's murder by the Ambans triggered it and that the Qianlong Emperor suppressed it. 'More than a hundred people killed, including the Ambans' as given.
The 1960s: the article says Lhasa City Municipal Construction Command built roads in 1964; left out. Lhasa City established January 1960; Chengguan District 23 April 1961 (left out).

Cultural Revolution is named only as the main period of damage ('mostly, but not solely'). The article does not say who destroyed what; none is attributed. The Barkhor demolition is 'in recent times' with no agent.

2008: 'the crackdown on protests in 2008' appears in the Economy section and 'the 2008 unrest' in the Barkhor paragraph; no figures or sides are given. The sentence about tourism falling follows the article.
The article gives the Lhasa Zhol Pillar's date as c. 764 CE and the capture of Chang'an as 763; kept as given. Qing 1720 entry and the 1751 Kashag as given. Ambans were sent 'by the Qing government'.
Ramoche statue: 'was said to have been found' kept as hedged in the article.
